title: The Prisoner Who Invented Modern Forensics
event_summary: Song Ci, a judicial intendant in southern China, published 'The Washing Away of Wrongs' (Xiyuan Jilu), the world's first systematic forensic science manual. Drawing on his experience investigating suspicious deaths across rural provinces, he documented methods for distinguishing drowning from strangulation, identifying poison, estimating time of death using insect activity, and even solving a murder by having villagers lay out their sickles in the sun until flies — attracted to invisible blood residue — landed on the guilty man's blade. The book codified forensic autopsy procedures that became mandatory across Chinese courts for centuries.
why_forgotten: Western histories of forensic science typically begin with 18th- and 19th-century European developments, crediting figures like Alphonse Bertillon or Edmond Locard as founders. Song Ci's work was not translated into European languages until the 20th century, and the broader pattern of attributing scientific innovation exclusively to the Western Enlightenment tradition erased China's five-century head start. Colonial-era academic frameworks systematically undervalued non-European contributions to empirical science.
why_it_matters: Song Ci's manual established foundational principles still used in modern forensic pathology: systematic crime scene investigation, entomological evidence for determining time of death, and the concept that physical evidence should override witness testimony. His insistence that every unnatural death required a trained coroner's examination prefigured the modern medicolegal system by half a millennium. Today's forensic entomology, toxicology, and evidence-based criminal justice all trace conceptual roots to procedures he first standardized in 1248.
